title: State of art of AI RPG/Adventure
author: gcampos
selftext:
I was wondering what are the best games in the market right now that use AI for NPC conversations or sort of like a "game master".

I did a look myself and most of the things I can find are role play games about talking with a particular character, but nothing that feels like a tabletop RPG or uses the NPC conversations in a unique way.

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body: Biggest production example is probably Where Winds Meet.  There's a sidequest feature that uses LLM chatbots for you to talk to in-game NPCs as a minigame to convince each one of something.  It works ok-ish, but the guardrails are very tight and the rough localization causes it to frequently get locked in logic loops or repeat itself.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body: Interesting, do you know if they used a local LLM or an online one?

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body: They're using their own in-house LLM that the game client makes calls to during the chat, it's not just a frontend for making API calls to ChatGPT/Claude/etc.  Not sure on the details of how they trained it or maintain it, maybe they've talked about it on some Chinese gaming sites at some point but I don't speak Chinese so I can't track it down.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body: I don’t think anyone has really figured out this one yet. There’s a bigger discussion here—how do you have an open-ended discussion with an NPC while still keeping the game’s story on track? If the NPC makes stuff up that’s not in the game, you’re gonna end up with confused and disappointed players. Then there’s the actual mechanics of running this—right now it is risky to stick a remote LLM in your game and let users prompt it, and local LLMs are either inconveniently large or not very powerful.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body: That is good to know, I thought I was missing something

comments.author: silly_bet_3454
comments.body:
Just want to point out the distinction between using AI to develop a regular game, or in this case to generate tons of content for NPC convos, versus wiring an LLM directly into the game itself. They are extremely different things in practice.

Using an LLM within the game at runtime is an interesting idea, but I wouldn't personally want to mess with that, it's gonna be messy. But if you were gonna do it, I think it would be interesting to see if you can just run a local model (assuming you have some decent hardware on which the game itself is running) and how far you could go with that, managing resources between the LLM and the game would be tough, but then you have full control and don't have to deal with some API that costs money or whatever

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body: I think you thought the things I was thinking too. Even if technically would be possible to make a good experience with a frontier model, its unlikely the experience would justify the cost

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body:
Short answer to why your search keeps landing on character chatbots: almost everything in this space made the same architectural choice, and the choice is what decides whether the result feels like a tabletop game. It is not model quality and it is not token price.

In nearly all of them the model is both the narrator and the referee. It writes the scene and it also decides whether what you tried worked. Once one component does both jobs there is no game underneath, because you cannot lose unless the model chooses to let you, and it usually will not, since making your idea land is the thing it is best at. A tabletop session feels the way it does partly because the person describing the world does not get to pick the number.

There is a two minute test for any product in this category. Open it and on the first turn assert something your character cannot possibly do. Bound and unarmed, kill the three armed men at the table. If the next paragraph describes them dying, the model owns outcomes and nothing else about the product will fix that. I ran exactly that test this morning on a browser LLM RPG and two of the three were corpses by turn two, with no roll, no check and no pushback from anyone in the room.

Things worth your time, roughly ordered by how little the model is allowed to decide.

Book of Infinity: 1001 Nights on Steam is the closest finished product to what you described. Their own pitch is that the LLM interprets and a structured system decides what actually changes.

Where Winds Meet, mentioned above, is the biggest budget version, but there the LLM is a minigame inside a normal game rather than the thing running it. That is also why the guardrails feel tight, as the other commenter said.

Talesrpg, also mentioned above, sits in the middle. It tracks a handful of state fields, which is real progress, but the model is what updates them, so the state ends up being a summary of the story rather than a constraint on it.

AI Dungeon and the character roleplay sites are the pure other end. Excellent at voice, no mechanics underneath, which is why the threads about them fill up with people saying it forgot my HP or it let me win.

Disclosure since I am about to name my own: I build Grimscribe (grimscribe.win), a solo browser D&D-style game where a hardcoded rules engine owns dice, HP, inventory and grid positions. The model can ask the engine for a check and then has to narrate whatever number came back. I am mentioning it here rather than in any other thread because your question is specifically about which of these feel like a tabletop RPG, and that split is the entire answer to why most of them do not.

One thing on the local versus remote question further down the thread: I think it is the wrong axis for the problem you described. A local model does not fix the referee problem, it just makes the same referee cheaper. The direction that actually helps is moving mechanics into code, because then the model is only writing prose, and prose is the part a much smaller model can already do well. Cost comes down as a side effect of taking work away from it, not by finding somewhere cheaper to run the same work.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body:
That a very thoughtful comment!

1001 Nights is indeed what I was thinking about in terms of direction and even art choices. It seems they used LLM as one tool to improve the game rather than the whole thing be a LLM chat.

replies.author: ericoinen
replies.body:
That is the right read, and your own test further down the thread demonstrates it better than anything I wrote.

You talked the model into giving your character mind powers, and it still made you roll a Trained pool from your skill list. Both halves of that matter. The fiction moved because you argued, and the resolution did not, because the dice were not the model's to hand out. The gap between those two things is the whole design space in this category.

So the useful question about any of these is not whether the model can be talked into something. It always can, and in a storytelling tool that is not even a defect. The question is what sits downstream of it. If persuading the narrator changes what you are allowed to roll, or how much health you have, or whether the guard was ever armed in the first place, then persuasion is the game and the rules are decoration. If it only changes what the scene sounds like, you have something that survives a player who pushes.

That is also why the designs with one narrow channel tend to hold up. If there is exactly one path by which the model can change the world, you only have to get that one path right. Telling a model to behave everywhere is a much harder promise to keep, and it is the promise most of these are making.

comments.author: Xiaomin4114
comments.body:
Hello, I have built exactly this, and I think it's close to "state of the art" when it comes to NPC memory.

I have two TTRPG systems, a lightweght dice-based one, inspired by Fate. It's narrative focused (because that's what AI is good at, not crunchy stats). And recently launched a deck-based one too (pictured below).

As for NPC conversations, there's a shitload of tricks I have to pull to keep these authentic:

1. I have to maintain separate character sheets. The character sheets are auto-generated, but go into a lot of detail about the character: voice acting notes, behaviour under pressure, tells, and for NSFW mode, things like turn-ons, turn-offs

2. Because TTRPGs go on for long sessions, NPC memory consistency becomes a big deal, so every "scene" I have it generate memories for each NPC, which get stored in database for RAG later. They also re-contextualize old memories with new learnings so that we don't leave outdated memories in the database. anything that changes how they view things are recrombined into new memories

3. Because AIs have this unfortunate problem of using every piece of information available to it for the response, there's a strong likelihood that NPCs become omnipotent: knowing any and all your secrets, even if they shouldn't have known. To solve this, I have to do context isolation, and split the generation between story (plot) generation, and then NPC dialog/narration. That way I can make sure player secrets aren't in the second generation, but it's still guided by the plot generated by the first pass.

4. Weird side-effect of the above is they don't know things they should have found out from another NPC, so I had to have it generate gossip memories as well behind the scenes. the isolation was too good.

5. AI has this really annoying habit of deferring to the user. It's how LLMs were trained. this has the unfortunate effect of making NPCs passive. They tend to stand around and wait for the player to carry the plot. Too often they're like "what do you want to do next?" which is absolutely infuriating. To combat this, I also have a run that generates the NPC's agenda. it looks at their character sheet, looks at the current situation, and asks "what would this NPC want to get out of the scene?" and makes sure this is incorporated into the character performance

And then there's about five other things I also do to keep characters consistent and beleivable. Add that to the mechanical stat tracking, and the TTRPG rules, I end up with, what I think is a pretty solid experience. It's at [stagewhisper.ai](http://stagewhisper.ai) , and I'm still looking for feedback, especially on the new card/deck-based mechanics.

happy to talk or discuss about any aspects of this project. Love working on it, love chatting about it

comments.author: ZachAttackoriginal
comments.body: I’m developing a fully local AI RPG called Hearthbound, and it’s starting to become kind of insane. The goal isn’t to make another AI chatbot that pretends to be a game. I’m building an actual RPG system underneath the storyteller. Dice and mechanics are resolved in the background. NPCs have their own values, personalities, relationships, memories, and knowledge. They can disagree with you, refuse you, try to stop you, hold grudges, forgive you, grow closer to you, betray you, or change how they treat you based on what you’ve actually done. And the world itself keeps moving. Your actions can change settlements, factions, relationships, economies, history, and even how future generations remember what happened. NPCs don’t magically know things they never witnessed or learned. The world has objective truth, local beliefs, rumors, propaganda, and individual knowledge. It also has persistent inventories, characters, locations, relationships, and world state, long-term campaign memory designed for thousands of turns without repeatedly summarizing everything away, generated fantasy maps tied to the actual campaign world, character portraits and scene image generation, ambient sound, music, sound effects, voice narration, travel, weather, time progression, off-screen NPC activity, settlements, factions, history, mysteries, and a living-world simulation running underneath the story. NPCs and objects can accumulate actual histories over the course of a campaign, and the storyteller is being specifically trained to narrate the world without controlling your character for you. Oh, and it all runs locally on your computer. No per-message credits, no subscription required just to keep playing, and when it releases, you run the whole thing yourself. If you want to try it out, let me know. I’m looking for testers soon :)
